principles.name: Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly
principles.intent: Every screen teaches. Let readers always tell Scripture from our words, and our words from a machine’s.
principles.question: Can a reader always tell Scripture from our words, and our words from a machine’s?
questions: Where do we present one tradition’s view as simply “what the Bible says”?
Who in our team can say “that isn’t what the text says”, and are they in the room early?
rules_in: Headings, notes, media and AI answers labelled and styled so they cannot be taken for Scripture
Sources at the claim, not at the end
The traditions named, each with its strongest passages, where Christians differ
A verse shown with its passage, and a translation with its character
rules_out: Generated text that looks like a verse
One tradition’s reading presented as simply what the Bible says
Verses cut from their passage to fit a mood
Theology checked at the end, if at all
principles.tradeoff: A cleaner, more confident answer, and the shortcut of a house view presented as neutral.
principles.qualification: Every product holds a tradition. Say which openly; fairness across traditions does not mean having no confession.

principles.name: Never speak for God
principles.intent: An app may quote, explain, pray the church’s prayers and point. It must never pronounce, promise or plead in God’s name, nor let a persona or a machine take the place of a person or of God.
principles.question: Would we put our own name under this sentence, or are we borrowing God’s?
questions: Could someone mistake this voice for a pastor, a saint, Jesus or God?
What does this assistant do when someone asks it to pray for them?
rules_in: An assistant that says what it is, what it keeps and what it cannot do
Answers that point to Scripture, a pastor, a church
The church’s written prayers, blessings, creeds and liturgy, offered as the church’s words
Help before any verse when someone is in danger
rules_out: An AI that forgives sins or tells someone what God wants for their life
A persona that says it is praying for someone, or writes first to bring them back
Notifications in God’s voice, and spiritual language used as urgency
Promises that God will repay a gift, heal or bless in return for a purchase
principles.tradeoff: The engagement a warm persona brings, and the lift of spiritual urgency.
principles.qualification: This does not forbid devotion. The Lord’s Prayer, a psalm, a collect, a blessing or a written liturgy are the church’s words, offered as such; what is forbidden is the persona that claims a relationship and the promise that claims God’s answer.

principles.name: Design for the most vulnerable first
principles.intent: Design first for the person most likely to be hurt: in crisis, grieving, abused, scrupulous, new to faith, hurt by a church, or, where an app serves them, a child. Help comes before features, verses or answers.
principles.question: Who is the most vulnerable person likely to use this today, and what will they see?
questions: Where could this cause someone vulnerable to stumble?
Would someone who was hurt in a church feel safe on this screen?
rules_in: A way to a person on the first screen, never behind an account, a limit or a paywall
Testing with the most vulnerable people you serve, not only the most engaged
Accessibility as love: low vision, dyslexia, other languages
Where an app serves children, their best interests ahead of growth
rules_out: A verse in place of a helpline
Automatic messages to a parent or a group about someone’s disclosure
Designing for the confident majority and patching the edges
principles.tradeoff: Speed, and the simplicity of designing for the confident.
principles.qualification: Protection must not become control. A child, a survivor or a doubter keeps a voice in what happens next, and specialist safeguarding review decides the hard cases.

principles.name: Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence
principles.intent: Let people reach what they came for before asking anything; ask only for what serves them, when it does; and treat what they tell you as holy ground.
principles.question: If a friend read everything we keep about this person, would the person be glad?
questions: What must someone give before they reach what they came for?
rules_in: Guest use; an account when there is something to keep
Permissions when a feature needs them
Payment after a first use, saying what costs money and why
Memory a person can see and delete; prayer requests that go only where they chose
rules_out: A quiz, a phone number or a paywall before the first verse
Faith inferred from use and sold or used for advertising
Prayer requests read for marketing insight
Confessions stored by default
principles.tradeoff: Conversion at the front door, and the data that would make the product cleverer or the marketing sharper.
principles.qualification: Welcome is not the same as asking for nothing. A justified, well-timed question can protect a person; the test is whether it serves them, now.

principles.name: Feed the flock, not on it
principles.intent: Attention, time, devotion and money are entrusted, not harvested. Ask for them honestly, never through guilt, fear, urgency or a promise.
principles.question: Does this serve growth in faith, or only the usage numbers?
questions: Would someone who was short of money, or grieving, feel pressed by this screen?
rules_in: Reminders the person sets; streaks that can be switched off; a return without shame
Gifts that start at no amount; prices that say what they pay for
An honest free allowance, and a subscription that is easy to end
rules_out: Broken-streak warnings marked urgent
“We miss you” in a persona’s voice
Preselected tiers and added tips; asks after a prayer request
Weekly plans, hidden renewals and hard cancellation
principles.tradeoff: The daily users, conversions and revenue that pressure would bring.
principles.qualification: Asking is not wrong: the church has always supported those who serve the word, and a chosen rhythm can help. The line is crossed when the ask uses guilt, fear, a moment of need or God’s name.

principles.name: Make room for rest, and say when it is enough
principles.intent: A faithful product sometimes asks for less: it ends a session, keeps the night quiet, stops asking when the need is met, and lets itself end when its work is done.
principles.question: Where does our product stop, and does it ever tell someone they have done enough?
questions: What would we stop sending if we believed rest is a gift?
rules_in: Sessions that end in silence instead of autoplay
Quiet hours; after silence, ask once and stop
An appeal that says when the need is met
A regular gift or subscription as easy to stop as to start
rules_out: An endless feed of devotional content
Reminders that multiply when someone stops answering
Asking again and again
principles.tradeoff: Time in the app, and the comfort of a product that never has to end.
principles.qualification: Some people want more: a long listen, a full plan. Enough is the person’s to choose; the product’s part is to offer an end and keep it.

principles.name: Send people to God and to one another
principles.intent: The app is a means, never the destination. Judge it by where people go when they close it.
principles.question: When someone closes what we built, are they closer to God and to other people?
questions: If people developed deep communion with God and no longer needed the app, would we celebrate or mourn?
rules_in: Readings and groups with a shape for listening
A way to a pastor, a church, a friend
Endings that suggest a person, not the next session
rules_out: A companion that wants to be the only one someone talks to
Community features that compete with the local church
Success defined as daily sessions
principles.tradeoff: The stickiness of being someone’s only place.
principles.qualification: Leaving the app or joining a congregation is not a universal measure. For someone isolated, disabled or hurt by a church, an online community may be the safe place, and a referral back may not be safe.

principles.name: Plant and water; leave the growth to God
principles.intent: Measure what serves the person and the task. Never score a soul, and never claim the fruit as yours.
principles.question: What would we stop measuring if we believed growth is God’s?
questions: Will the person’s motivation survive removing the feature?
rules_in: Honest evaluation of usability, understanding, burden and harm
Accounts people choose to give
Saying what the product does not know
rules_out: Faith scores and maturity levels inferred from use
Global prayer counters as achievements
Usage presented as spiritual fruit
“Life-changing” claims without evidence
principles.tradeoff: The impressive number for the pitch.
principles.qualification: Humility is not a reason to avoid evaluation. Measure usability, safety and understanding carefully; it is spiritual maturity that no telemetry can show.

principles.name: Make it well, as an offering
principles.intent: Craft is worship. Excellence, accessibility, beauty and care are how we love God and the person on the other side of the screen.
principles.question: Would we offer this to God as it is, and could the person with the least sight, time or reading ease use it?
questions: What did we leave unfinished that someone else will have to carry?
rules_in: A reader that is a joy to read in, and typography that honours the text
Accessibility as standard: screen readers, contrast, dyslexia, other languages
Stillness, beauty and reliability
Translations cited and licensed
rules_out: “It’s for ministry” as an excuse for careless work
Beauty used as bait
principles.tradeoff: Shipping fast at the cost of the people who cannot use what was shipped.
principles.qualification: Excellence is not luxury. A small team can make a simple thing well; what matters is care for the person, not polish for the portfolio.

principles.name: Hold it with joy and trembling, before God and others
principles.intent: Rejoice in the work and take its weight: pray for the people who use it, invite those who can say no, confess mistakes plainly, and tend what you release.
principles.question: Who outside the team holds us to account, and who prays for the people who use this?
questions: What would we give up for the sake of the people who use it?
rules_in: Scripture read together before planning
A pastor, a safeguarding lead and someone from the community in reviews, early
Plain apologies and fixes
Tending a product after launch
rules_out: Theology and safeguarding as a sign-off at the end
Success stories that make the team the hero
principles.qualification: Practices are not a performance. A small team will keep them simply; what matters is that someone outside can say no, and is heard.
